Models chain into pipelines. Here is long-form Russian speech recognition with GigaAM, segmented by FireRedVAD: let model = GigaAm::from_hub_with_revision("vpermilp/GigaAM-v3", "ctc")?; let bounds = EncoderBounds { sample_rate: model.config.sample_rate as u32, hop_length: model.config.hop_length, subsampling_factor: model.config.subsampling_factor, max_mel_frames: model.config.max_mel_frames, recommended_target_secs: model.recommended_chunk_secs(), }; let splitter = FireRedVadSplitter::from_hub(&bounds)?; let mut asr = Asr::assemble(splitter, |max_chunk| GigaAmTranscriber::new(model, opts, max_chunk))?; let result = asr.transcribe_default(&waveform)?; Any ONNX model can be compiled once and replayed. The graph is traced on your input tensor, so new data written into it is seen by every replay: let proto = ModelProto::decode(std::fs::read("model.onnx")?.as_slice())?; let input = Tensor::from_ndarray(&first_batch); // [1, 3, 224, 224] f32 let OnnxModel { outputs, .. } = OnnxImporter::new().import_model_with_inputs( proto, HashMap::from([("input".to_string(), input.clone())]), &[("batch", 1)], )?; let plan = Tensor::prepare_batch(outputs.values())?; // compile once plan.execute()?; for batch in batches { input.array_view_mut::<f32>()?.as_slice_mut().unwrap().copy_from_slice(&batch); plan.execute()?; // replay: no tracing, no compilation, no allocation }

The Nix flake pins every compiler and library, and CI uses the same flake: nix develop # development shell nix flake check # the CI suite: clippy, nextest (with Z3 and proptest), fmt Without Nix you need the following: Dependency Version Required Purpose Rust 1.88+ yes Edition 2024 LLVM ≥ 16 yes CPU code generation; libLLVM is loaded at runtime Clang — yes GPU kernel compilation, C backend, fallback when libLLVM is missing protobuf, pkgconf, zlib, libffi, libxml2 — yes ONNX protos and the LLVM toolchain Z3 ≥ 4.15 no Rewrite verification (--features z3) NVIDIA driver CUDA ≥ 12.0 (R525) no CUDA backend amdgpu kernel driver (KFD) — no AMD backend cargo test --workspace cargo test --workspace --features z3,proptest SVOD_THREADS sets the single thread budget used to compile kernels and run CPU kernels.

AOT compilation: serialize optimized graphs and compiled kernels, so a model starts instantly and runs where no compiler is available (e.g. WASM). Data analysis primitives: FlashAttention-style GPU kernels for k-means, kNN, PCA, SVD, (H)DBSCAN, UMAP and t-SNE on every backend. Formal verification of generated code: annotated C output that proves the absence of out-of-bounds accesses and lossy casts. More hardware: server (MI300–MI450, H100–B200), consumer (Ryzen AI, Apple M3–M5, RTX 30–50) and embedded (Snapdragon X, RK3588) targets behind one tensor API, plus a userspace AMD driver with no dependency on the AMD software stack.
MIT

svod-model ships pure-Rust ports of pretrained models. Each one downloads its weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, compiles its graph once through jit_wrapper!, and is checked against the upstream PyTorch implementation in the crate's tests. svod-arch adds the host-side machinery around them: CTC / RN-T decoders, VAD chunking and the long-form audio pipeline. Domain Model Module Weights Speech recognition GigaAM v3 (CTC, RN-T) gigaam vpermilp/GigaAM-v3 Speech recognition Whisper (tiny … large-v3, turbo) whisper vpermilp/whisper Voice activity FireRedVAD (batch, streaming) firered_vad vpermilp/firered_vad Voice activity Silero VAD 16k silero_vad vpermilp/silero-vad Speech enhancement GTCRN gtcrn vpermilp/gtcrn Speaker diarization DiariZen (WavLM + Conformer) diarizen BUT-FIT/diarizen-wavlm-large-s80-md-v2 Speaker diarization Nemotron-3-Diarization (offline, streaming; up to 8 speakers) nemotron_diar nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization Speaker embedding WeSpeaker ResNet34 wespeaker pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM Text embeddings BGE-M3 (dense, sparse, ColBERT), BGE-reranker-v2-m3 bgem3 BAAI/bge-m3, BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 Text embeddings Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B qwen3 Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Text embeddings, fill-mask ModernBERT base / large modernbert answerdotai/ModernBERT-base Vision ResNet 18 / 34 / 50 / 101 / 152 resnet timm/resnet*.a1_in1k Vision YOLO26 (detect, cls, seg, obb, pose, depth, semseg) yolo ultralytics/yolo26n … yolo26x The model crate README lists the upstream repositories and the parity tests behind each row.

[dependencies] svod-model = "0.2" svod-arch = "0.2" # Asr, splitters, decoders svod-tensor = "0.2" svod-dtype = "0.2" The build needs LLVM and Clang on the machine (see the introduction); nothing else is required for the CPU. GPU backends are compiled in and register themselves when the driver is present — pick one with SVOD_DEVICE: SVOD_DEVICE=CUDA:0 cargo run --release -p svod-model --example whisper_infer -- audio.wav SVOD_DEVICE=AMD:0 cargo run --release -p svod-model --example gigaam_infer -- audio.wav Weights land in the Hugging Face cache (HF_HUB_CACHE, or ~/.cache/huggingface by default; HF_TOKEN for gated repositories). Compiled kernels are cached in ~/.cache/svod/objects, so the second start of a process skips compilation.

Every example is a complete program under model/examples and is the best starting point for the model it drives. All audio examples expect 16 kHz mono WAV. cargo run -p svod-model --release --example gigaam_infer -- audio.wav [--rnnt] [--timestamps] cargo run -p svod-model --release --example whisper_infer -- audio.wav [--size base] [--language auto] [--timestamps] cargo run -p svod-model --release --example vad_stream -- audio.wav # streaming VAD events cargo run -p svod-model --release --example vad_bench -- audio.wav # Silero vs FireRedVAD cargo run -p svod-model --release --example gtcrn_enhance -- --in noisy.wav --out clean.wav --hub cargo run -p svod-model --release --example nemotron_diarize -- audio.wav [--stream low|very-low|ultra-low] cargo run -p svod-model --release --example qwen3_embed -- --texts texts.txt --batch 8 --max-len 512 cargo run -p svod-model --release --example resnet_classify -- --hub --image dog.bin --side 224 cargo run -p svod-model --release --example yolo_detect -- --hub --scale small --image photo.bin --side 640 Image inputs are raw f32 NCHW files (3 × side × side × 4 bytes, normalized to 0–1); the examples synthesize a pattern when --image is omitted, so every command above runs without assets. --profile on the speech and embedding examples prints a per-stage report with device time, roofline GFLOP/s and GB/s per kernel. With SVOD_ORIGIN=1 each kernel is attributed to the model code that produced it, and --origin-depth N rolls the report up to module depth N: SVOD_ORIGIN=1 cargo run -p svod-model --release --example gigaam_infer -- \ audio.wav --profile --origin-depth 3 --profile-json profile.json

Long-form transcription is a pipeline: a VAD splits the waveform into speech chunks sized to the encoder, each chunk is transcribed, and the pieces are stitched back with timestamps. Asr::assemble wires the two halves so the transcriber's JIT is prepared once at the chunk size the splitter can emit: use svod_arch::pipelines::audio::{Asr, RunOptions}; use svod_model::audio::EncoderBounds; use svod_model::firered_vad::FireRedVadSplitter; use svod_model::gigaam::{GigaAm, GigaAmTranscriber, TranscribeOpts}; let model = GigaAm::from_hub_with_revision("vpermilp/GigaAM-v3", "ctc")?; // "e2e_rnnt" for RN-T let bounds = EncoderBounds { sample_rate: model.config.sample_rate as u32, hop_length: model.config.hop_length, subsampling_factor: model.config.subsampling_factor, max_mel_frames: model.config.max_mel_frames, recommended_target_secs: model.recommended_chunk_secs(), }; let splitter = FireRedVadSplitter::from_hub(&bounds)?; let opts = TranscribeOpts::default(); let mut asr = Asr::assemble(splitter, |max_chunk| GigaAmTranscriber::new(model, opts, max_chunk))?; let result = asr.transcribe(&waveform, RunOptions { words: true, ..Default::default() })?; println!("{}", result.text); for chunk in &result.chunks { for word in chunk.words.iter().flatten() { println!("[{:.2} - {:.2}] {}", chunk.start_sec + word.start, chunk.start_sec + word.end, word.text); } } The head (CTC or RN-T) follows the weights revision. TranscribeOpts holds the structural choices — beam_decode and the SDPA scores budget max_scores_mib — while RunOptions (words, segments, profile) is a per-call switch, so one Asr serves every mode. FireRedVadSplitter::builder() exposes the chunking knobs (threshold, min_duration, max_duration, target_duration, …); SVOD_VAD_THRESHOLD and SVOD_VAD_TARGET_CHUNK_SECS override the defaults from the environment. Swap in FixedLengthSplitter or SileroVadSplitter without touching the transcriber.

Whisper decodes fixed 30-second windows, so the splitter is a FixedLengthSplitter. The transcriber runs mel → encoder → cached beam decoding with temperature fallback, then DTW word alignment on request: use svod_arch::pipelines::audio::{Asr, FixedLengthSplitter, RunOptions}; use svod_model::whisper::{ CHUNK_LENGTH, DecodeOptions, DecodeStrategy, ModelDimensions, SAMPLE_RATE, Whisper, WhisperAlignedTranscriber, WhisperSize, WhisperTokenizer, }; let size = WhisperSize::Base; let dims = ModelDimensions::for_size(size); let model = Whisper::from_hub("vpermilp/whisper", size.name(), dims)?; let tokenizer = WhisperTokenizer::from_hub(model.is_multilingual(), model.dims.num_languages())?; let options = DecodeOptions { language: None, // detect strategy: DecodeStrategy::Beam { size: 5 }, ..Default::default() }; let window = CHUNK_LENGTH * SAMPLE_RATE; let transcriber = WhisperAlignedTranscriber::new(model, tokenizer, options, size, window)?; let mut asr = Asr::new(FixedLengthSplitter::new(window, SAMPLE_RATE), transcriber); let result = asr.transcribe(&waveform, RunOptions::default())?; println!("{}", result.text); WhisperSize::from_name("large-v3") parses the CLI spelling, and WhisperPlan (encoder_batch, decoder_slots, alignment_batch) sizes the compiled graphs when the defaults do not fit the device.

FireRedVadStreamer is the streaming front-end: feed samples as they arrive, get speech boundaries back as events. The conv caches recycle on the device between pushes, so each chunk_frames of audio costs one small dispatch: use svod_model::firered_vad::{FireRedVadStreamer, VadEvent}; let mut vad = FireRedVadStreamer::from_hub()?; // or builder().model(m).chunk_frames(16).build() for block in waveform.chunks(1600) { // 100 ms at 16 kHz for event in vad.push(block)? { match event { VadEvent::SpeechStart { frame } => println!("start {:.2}s", frame as f32 / 100.0), VadEvent::SpeechEnd { start_frame, end_frame } => println!("end {:.2}s", end_frame as f32 / 100.0), } } } let flush = vad.flush()?; // closes the last segment for (start, end) in &flush.timestamps { // seconds println!("{start:.2}s - {end:.2}s"); } GTCRN speech enhancement is one JIT over STFT → network → ISTFT. The GRU recurrence unrolls per frame, so the example runs it in fixed 128-frame chunks with one prepare: use svod_model::gtcrn::{Gtcrn, GtcrnJit, HOP}; use svod_model::jit::InputSpec; const CHUNK: usize = 128 * HOP; let mut jit = GtcrnJit::new(Gtcrn::from_hub()?); jit.prepare(InputSpec::f32(&[1, CHUNK]))?; let mut out = vec![0.0f32; CHUNK]; for chunk in waveform.chunks(CHUNK) { // pad the last one to CHUNK jit.waveform_mut()?.copyin(bytemuck::cast_slice(chunk))?; jit.execute()?; jit.output()?.copyout(bytemuck::cast_slice_mut(&mut out))?; }

nemotron_diar runs Nemotron-3-Diarization: per 10 ms frame, the activity of up to 8 speakers, numbered by first appearance. Recordings and live streams run the same loop — the audio is cut into chunks, each encoded together with a speaker cache of earlier frames — and differ only in chunk sizes (offline, or the model card's 1.04 / 0.64 / 0.32 s latencies): use svod_arch::diarization::{Binarization, write_rttm}; use svod_dtype::DType; use svod_model::nemotron_diar::{Diarizer, NemotronDiar, StreamingMode}; // Whole recording. let mut diarizer = Diarizer::offline(NemotronDiar::from_hub(DType::BFloat16, 1)?)?; let result = diarizer.diarize(&waveform, 16000)?; // probs: [frames, 8], 10 ms rows write_rttm(std::io::stdout(), "meeting", &result.segments(&Binarization::default()))?; // Live stream, 1.04 s latency. let model = NemotronDiar::from_hub(DType::BFloat16, 1)?; let mut diarizer = Diarizer::streaming(model, StreamingMode::LowLatency)?; let mut session = diarizer.session(); for block in microphone { session.push(&block)?; diarizer.run(&mut [&mut session])?; let probs = session.take_probs(); // rows emitted since the last call } session.finish(); diarizer.run(&mut [&mut session])?; run takes any number of sessions and batches their ready chunks, up to the max_batch passed to from_hub. svod_arch::diarization holds the model-agnostic parts: the speaker cache, the thresholds turning probabilities into segments, and RTTM output.

The vision models are a single jit_wrapper! each: one images input, a batch_var so one plan serves every batch size up to max_batch_size, and one output. Image size is baked in at prepare: use svod_dtype::DType; use svod_model::jit::InputSpec; use svod_model::resnet::{OutputMode, ResNet, ResNetDepth, ResNetJit}; let model = ResNet::from_hub("timm/resnet50.a1_in1k", ResNetDepth::R50, OutputMode::Classification { num_classes: 1000 })?; let mut jit = ResNetJit::new(model); jit.prepare(InputSpec::new(&[1, 3, 224, 224], DType::Float32))?; jit.images_mut()?.copyin(bytemuck::cast_slice(&nchw_pixels))?; // [1, 3, 224, 224] f32 jit.execute_bound(1)?; // batch = 1 let logits = jit.logits_to_vec::<f32>()?; // [1000] This is the wrapper behind it, verbatim: jit_wrapper! { ResNetJit(ResNet) { inputs { images: Tensor } batch_var b: (1, model.config.max_batch_size), outputs { logits } build(images) { model.forward(images) } } } YOLO26 follows the same shape. The detection head returns decoded xyxy boxes with class scores, [B, 4 + nc, anchors], and postprocess_raw does the top-k selection: use svod_model::yolo::{Yolo26Detect, Yolo26DetectJit, YoloConfig, YoloScale, postprocess_raw}; let cfg = YoloConfig::new(YoloScale::Nano, 80); let mut jit = Yolo26DetectJit::new(Yolo26Detect::from_hub("ultralytics/yolo26n", cfg)?); jit.prepare(InputSpec::f32(&[1, 3, 640, 640]))?; jit.images_mut()?.copyin(bytemuck::cast_slice(&nchw_pixels))?; jit.execute_bound(1)?; let detections = postprocess_raw(&jit.predictions_to_vec::<f32>()?, &jit.predictions_shape()?, 80, 300)?; for [x1, y1, x2, y2, conf, class] in &detections[0] { println!("class {} {conf:.2} at ({x1:.0}, {y1:.0})-({x2:.0}, {y2:.0})", *class as usize); }

The text models take token ids; tokenization stays with the caller (the qwen3_embed example implements Qwen2's byte-level BPE on tiktoken-rs from the published tokenizer.json). Qwen3Embedder packs rows into batches of max_batch × max_len and keeps one prepared plan per batch shape: use svod_model::qwen3::{Qwen3Embedder, Qwen3Embedding, qwen3_embedding_0_6b}; let config = qwen3_embedding_0_6b(); // bf16 on a tensor-core GPU, else f32 let model = Qwen3Embedding::from_hub("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B", config)?; let mut embedder = Qwen3Embedder::new(model, 8, 512); // batch, max_len let rows: Vec<Vec<u32>> = texts.iter().map(|t| tokenize(t)).collect(); let embeddings: Vec<Vec<f32>> = embedder.embed(&rows)?; // L2-normalized, one row per text BgeM3Embedder (encode_dense, encode_colbert, encode with sparse weights), the BGE and Qwen3 rerankers and ModernBert follow the same from_hub(model_id, config) convention; svod_model::default_compute_dtype() picks bf16 where the device has bf16 tensor cores and f32 otherwise.

A new model is a #[derive(Module)] struct whose forward is written against the tensor API, loaded with svod_model::state::load_safetensors, and wrapped once in jit_wrapper! for inference. JIT graphs covers the wrapper — symbolic batch variables, on-device recurrent state and the data-independence contract — and Kernel origins shows how to read the profiler against your module tree.

svod-onnx turns a .onnx file into the same lazy tensor graph a hand-written model builds: every operator is decomposed into svod-tensor operations, so the imported graph goes through the full scheduler, optimizer and code generator and runs on every backend. There is no ONNX Runtime underneath. Capability Status Forward inference Supported Operators 162 / 200 standard ops (parity table) Conformance 1357 ONNX backend node tests pass on both CPU backends (Clang, LLVM); the suite also runs on AMD and CUDA when SVOD_DEVICE selects one Dynamic dimensions Bound at import time (see Dynamic dimensions) Microsoft contrib ops Attention, RotaryEmbedding, SkipLayerNormalization, EmbedLayerNormalization, BiasGelu, FastGelu Training / backward pass Not supported For an operator outside the table, ort (a wrapper around the C++ ONNX Runtime) covers the full specification.

[dependencies] svod-onnx = "0.2" svod-tensor = "0.2" prost = "0.14" # ModelProto::decode The importer has three entry points: Call Weights Inputs import(path, dim_bindings) Float initializers are memory-mapped lazily from the file; data_location = EXTERNAL resolves against the file's directory Unallocated placeholders you assign to import_model_with_inputs(proto, inputs, dim_bindings) Read from the decoded ModelProto Your own tensors, traced into the graph directly import_model(proto, dim_bindings) Read from the decoded ModelProto Placeholders, as import All three return an OnnxModel: pub struct OnnxModel { pub inputs: HashMap<String, Tensor>, // graph inputs that are not initializers pub outputs: HashMap<String, Tensor>, // lazy; nothing has run yet pub variables: HashMap<String, Variable>, // one per named dim_param }

Build the input tensors yourself and hand them to the importer. The graph is traced on them, so the tensors you hold are the buffers the kernels read: use std::collections::HashMap; use prost::Message; use svod_onnx::parser::onnx::ModelProto; use svod_onnx::{OnnxImporter, OnnxModel}; use svod_tensor::Tensor; fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let proto = ModelProto::decode(std::fs::read("model.onnx")?.as_slice())?; // Same shape and dtype as the graph input "input" let image = Tensor::from_ndarray(&load_image_nchw()); // [1, 3, 224, 224] f32 let OnnxModel { outputs, .. } = OnnxImporter::new().import_model_with_inputs( proto, HashMap::from([("input".to_string(), image.clone())]), &[("batch", 1)], )?; // Schedule every output together, run once Tensor::realize_batch(outputs.values())?; for (name, tensor) in &outputs { println!("{name}: {:?}", tensor.as_ndarray::<f32>()?); } Ok(()) } Tensor::from_ndarray and Tensor::from_raw_bytes(bytes, &dims, dtype) give a tensor that owns a buffer of the declared shape; Tensor::from_slice is always 1-D, so reshape it only through one of those.

For repeated inference compile the outputs into a plan and write new data straight into the input buffer between runs: let plan = Tensor::prepare_batch(outputs.values())?; // schedule + compile, once plan.execute()?; for batch in batches { image.array_view_mut::<f32>()?.as_slice_mut().unwrap().copy_from_slice(&batch); plan.execute()?; // replay: no tracing, no compilation let logits = outputs["output"].as_vec::<f32>()?; } array_view_mut is a zero-copy ndarray view over the input's host mapping; prepare_batch wires each output tensor to the plan's buffer, so as_vec / as_ndarray read the latest run.

import(path) is the entry point that memory-maps the weights and resolves external data. Its inputs are placeholders: assign a value of the same shape and realize the input before the outputs. A placeholder keeps one buffer across plans, so a prepared plan also sees later assign + realize calls and array_view_mut writes to it. let OnnxModel { mut inputs, outputs, .. } = OnnxImporter::new().import("model.onnx", &[])?; let input = inputs.remove("input").unwrap(); input.assign(&Tensor::from_ndarray(&image)); input.realize()?; Tensor::realize_batch(outputs.values())?; A model whose inputs are all initializers needs none of this: Tensor::realize_batch(model.outputs.values())? runs it.

A named dim_param ("batch", "sequence_length") becomes a Variable with bounds (1, default_max_dim); default_max_dim is a public field of OnnxImporter and defaults to 32767. An unnamed or zero-sized dimension becomes 1. Bind every dynamic dimension at import. A bound dimension is a plain constant in the traced graph, so the kernels specialize to it: let model = importer.import("model.onnx", &[("batch", 8), ("sequence_length", 512)])?; println!("{:?}", model.inputs["input_ids"]); // Tensor { shape: [8, 512], dtype: Scalar(Int64), .. } A dimension you leave unbound stays symbolic: its buffer is allocated for the upper bound and dims() fails with SymbolicShape (the Debug output prints shape: symbolic). Rebinding through ExecutionPlan::execute_with_vars is not supported for imported graphs — a bound dimension is already a constant, and an unbound one compiles a kernel that ignores the runtime value. To serve several batch sizes, import once per size, or lower default_max_dim so the unbound buffers stay small. Out-of-range bindings fail at import with IrConstruction; a binding for a name the model does not declare is ignored.

Parse. The protobuf is decoded, initializers become tensors, graph inputs become shape specs and the opset per domain is recorded. Through import, every float initializer with more than one element is a lazy view into the file (SHRINK → BITCAST → RESHAPE → COPY onto the default device), so a large model costs no host copy; scalars are folded into constants. Trace. Nodes are visited in topological order and each dispatches to its tensor implementation. The result is a set of lazy output tensors. A few operators read a data input at trace time — Reshape's shape, Tile's repeats, TopK's k, Range, ConstantOfShape, and the axes input of the reductions from opset 13 (ReduceSum) or 18 (the rest) — so those small tensors are realized during import. When one of them is a graph input, supply it through import_model_with_inputs.

About fifty operators map 1:1 to a tensor method: "Add" => x.try_add(y)? "Relu" => x.relu()? "Sigmoid" => x.sigmoid()? "Equal" => x.try_eq(y)? Operators with many optional attributes use the tensor crate's builders: x.conv() .weight(w) .maybe_bias(bias) .auto_pad(AutoPad::SameLower) .group(32) .maybe_dilations(Some(&[2, 2])) .call()? The rest are multi-step decompositions. Mod, for instance, picks one of four forms from the fmod attribute and the input dtype; the floating-point Python-style branch is x - floor(x / y) * y: let div = x.try_div(y)?; x.try_sub(&div.floor().try_mul(y)?)? floor() carries no ?: the rounding ops, cast, neg, abs, square and sign cannot fail. The bitwise operators behind BitwiseAnd/Or/Xor and BitShift are try_bitand, try_bitor, try_bitxor, try_shl and try_shr.

Attributes are popped as they are read — attrs.int("axis", -1), attrs.float("epsilon", 1e-5) — and attrs.done() returns UnhandledAttributes if any are left, so an attribute an implementation forgot is an import error rather than a silently wrong result. Operators switch behaviour on the opset their domain imports: Softmax and LogSoftmax default to axis 1 before opset 13 and -1 from 13; ReduceSum takes its axes as an input from opset 13 and the other reductions from 18. The "" and ai.onnx domains share one opset.

The com.microsoft contrib operators that ONNX Runtime exports: Operator Notes Attention Packed QKV with mask_index (1-D, 2-D or n-D), unidirectional, qkv_hidden_sizes and a past KV cache RotaryEmbedding Interleaved and non-interleaved SkipLayerNormalization Residual + LayerNorm; the optional mean / inverse-std outputs are zeros EmbedLayerNormalization Token + position + segment embeddings → LayerNorm; the mask input is ignored BiasGelu, FastGelu Fused bias + GELU The standard ai.onnx Attention supports grouped-query attention, causal masking, past KV caching, softcap, every qk_matmul_output_mode, softmax_precision, nonpad_kv_seqlen and 3-D inputs; its outputs are [output, present_key, present_value, qk].

Nothing executes at trace time, so the condition of an If node is unknown. The importer traces both branches and merges them with where_: ONNX: if condition { then_branch } else { else_branch } Svod: then_result.where_(&condition, else_result) where_ reads "keep self where the condition holds"; condition.select(&a, &b) is the same op spelled from the mask's side. The compiled graph then handles any condition value, with one constraint: both branches must produce the same shapes and dtypes. A shape-polymorphic If is rejected at import.

Loop and Scan: iterative control flow needs repeated tracing or unrolling. RNN, GRU and LSTM are native ops instead; their direction is inferred from W's leading dimension (bidirectional works, reverse runs forward) and the activations and clip attributes are ignored. Training: no backward pass, gradients or optimizers. Category Examples Why Dynamic quantization QuantizeLinear, DequantizeLinear, DynamicQuantizeLinear (QLinearConv, QLinearMatMul, ConvInteger and MatMulInteger are implemented) Not yet ported Sequence ops SequenceConstruct, SequenceAt Non-tensor types are outside the type system Random RandomNormal, RandomUniform, Bernoulli No stateful RNG in the graph Signal processing DFT, STFT, MelWeightMatrix Not wired to the importer (the tensor crate has stft / istft / mel_spectrogram) Text StringNormalizer, TfIdfVectorizer No string type

Per-node tracing. At trace level the importer realizes every node's output as it is traced and logs its shape and first five values — a numerical bisection tool for a model that produces wrong results. It breaks fusion, so use it only for debugging, and install a tracing-subscriber with an EnvFilter in your binary: RUST_LOG=svod_onnx::importer=trace cargo run Tracing happens inside the import call, so real input values appear only when the inputs are supplied through import_model_with_inputs; placeholder inputs trace as empty buffers. Inspecting the graph. Tensor's Debug prints shape, dtype, device and realization state, never the data: let model = importer.import("model.onnx", &[])?; for (name, tensor) in &model.inputs { println!("input {name}: {tensor:?}"); } println!("outputs: {:?}", model.outputs.keys().collect::<Vec<_>>()); println!("variables: {:?}", model.variables); Kernel attribution. Every kernel the importer produces records its ONNX node as its origin, so the profiler reports device time per node — see Kernel origins.

Aspect Detail Entry points import(path, dims), import_model_with_inputs(proto, inputs, dims), import_model(proto, dims) Runtime inputs Build the tensors, pass them to import_model_with_inputs, write through array_view_mut between runs Dynamic dims Bind at import: &[("batch", 8)]; one import per batch size Operators 162 / 200 (parity table) Conformance 1357 node tests on Clang and LLVM; AMD and CUDA via SVOD_DEVICE Extensions com.microsoft Attention, RotaryEmbedding, SkipLayerNormalization, EmbedLayerNormalization, BiasGelu, FastGelu Limitations No training, no Loop / Scan, no shape-polymorphic If, no runtime rebinding of dynamic dims Next: Tensor API for the graph these models land in, or Running models for the native ports.

A tk kernel is a Rust function that records a tile program with the Kernel builder. Every call appends one statement to the open block and returns a typed handle. A handle carries its tier (Gmem<T>, Shared<T>, Regs<T>) and element type (BF16, F16, F32, I32, Bool); a shared allocation is a SmemRef<T>. Shapes are checked when the statement is recorded. Scalars such as block indices, offsets and trip counts are Sc expressions built with ordinary operators.

y = 2·x + 1 over a [rows, 64] f32 matrix, 16 rows per block. The view's row bound makes the last block's rows past rows read as zero and drops their writes, so rows need not be a multiple of 16. use svod_tk::build::*; use svod_tk::interp::run; use svod_tk::ir::*; fn axpb(rows: usize) -> Program { let cols = 64; let mut k = Kernel::new("axpb"); let x = k.param::<F32>("x", ParamKind::In, rows * cols); let y = k.param::<F32>("y", ParamKind::Out, rows * cols); k.grid([Sc::from(rows.div_ceil(16)), Sc::from(1), Sc::from(1)]); k.warps(4); let row0 = k.block(0) * 16; let tile = |k: &mut Kernel, p: ParamRef<F32>| { let v = k.view(p, 0, [cols, 1], Shape::new(16, cols), [Some(Sc::from(rows)), None]); k.at(v, row0.clone(), 0) }; let xv = tile(&mut k, x); let v = k.load(xv); let two = k.fill::<F32>(Shape::new(16, cols), Const::Float(2.0)); let one = k.fill::<F32>(Shape::new(16, cols), Const::Float(1.0)); let v = k.mul_add(v, two, one); let yv = tile(&mut k, y); k.store(yv, v); k.finish() } // On the host, no GPU: one Vec<f64> per parameter in, every parameter out. let x: Vec<f64> = (0..40 * 64).map(f64::from).collect(); let out = run(&axpb(40), vec![x, vec![0.0; 40 * 64]], &[])?; assert_eq!(out[1][64 * 39 + 1], 2.0 * (64.0 * 39.0 + 1.0) + 1.0); view(param, offset, [row_stride, col_stride], shape, bounds) is a window into a parameter. at(view, rows, cols) moves it and keeps the bounds relative to the new origin.

c = a·bᵀ over bf16 a [m, k] and b [n, k], accumulated in f32. This is a reduced form of kernels/gemm.rs, which adds the epilogues (bias, activation, gated weights, scale, residual, f32 output), grouped tile order, split reductions, the warpgroup core and two-crew ping-pong. fn gemm_nt(m: usize, n: usize, kk: usize, [bm, bn, bk]: [usize; 3], stages: usize) -> Program { assert!(kk.is_multiple_of(bk), "k is a multiple of bk"); let mut k = Kernel::new("gemm_nt"); let a = k.param::<BF16>("a", ParamKind::In, m * kk); let b = k.param::<BF16>("b", ParamKind::In, n * kk); let c = k.param::<BF16>("c", ParamKind::Out, m * n); k.grid([Sc::from(m.div_ceil(bm)), Sc::from(n.div_ceil(bn)), Sc::from(1)]); k.warps(4); let (row0, col0) = (k.block(0) * bm, k.block(1) * bn); let bound = |len: usize, tile: usize| (!len.is_multiple_of(tile)).then(|| Sc::from(len)); let a_view = k.view(a, 0, [kk, 1], Shape::new(bm, bk), [bound(m, bm), None]); let a_view = k.at(a_view, row0.clone(), 0); let b_view = k.view(b, 0, [kk, 1], Shape::new(bn, bk), [bound(n, bn), None]); let b_view = k.at(b_view, col0.clone(), 0); let (sa, sb) = (Shape::new(bm, bk), Shape::new(bn, bk)); let a_s = k.smem::<BF16>("a_s", stages * sa.elems()); let b_s = k.smem::<BF16>("b_s", stages * sb.elems()); let acc = k.zeros::<F32>(Shape::new(bm, bn)); let [acc] = k.pipeline( kk / bk, stages, [acc], |k, step, slot| { let koff = step * bk; let a_g = k.at(a_view, 0, koff.clone()); let a_t = k.smem_slot(a_s, slot.clone(), sa); k.stage(a_t, a_g, CopyMode::Async); let b_g = k.at(b_view, 0, koff); let b_t = k.smem_slot(b_s, slot, sb); k.stage(b_t, b_g, CopyMode::Async); }, |k, _step, slot, [acc]| { let a_t = k.smem_slot(a_s, slot.clone(), sa); let b_t = k.smem_slot(b_s, slot, sb); [k.mma(acc, a_t, false, b_t, true)] }, ); let out = k.cast::<F32, BF16>(acc); let c_view = k.view(c, 0, [n, 1], Shape::new(bm, bn), [bound(m, bm), bound(n, bn)]); let c_view = k.at(c_view, row0, col0); k.store(c_view, out); k.finish() } Bounds instead of padding. bound(len, tile) is Some(len) only where the tile grid overhangs len, so any m and n run without a copy. Only k must be a multiple of bk. The pipeline. pipeline(extent, stages, init, produce, consume) declares a producer and a consumer over a ring of stages shared slots (a Ring { stages, unroll, crews } also copies the loop once per slot or runs two crews), carrying init (here the accumulator) through the consumer. The author says what to copy into a slot and what to compute from it. The schedule template decides how far ahead copies run and places every wait and barrier. The product. mma(acc, a, a_t, b, b_t) is acc + A·B on f32 accumulators (i32 over 8-bit integers, MmaIn::Acc), here with B read transposed. It never names an instruction: the lowering picks the target's matrix-core atom and gives a, b and acc its layouts. The result is rounded once, at the cast before the store.

launch::graph_launch takes one tensor per declared parameter, in order, and returns the first output as a lazy Tensor. The kernel runs when the result is realized, like any graph kernel. The library GEMM takes a GemmCfg, whose lowering needs the device's measured costs. use svod_dtype::{DType, default_device::default_device}; use svod_tensor::Tensor; use svod_tk::atoms::{Core, Device, Target}; use svod_tk::build::BF16; use svod_tk::kernels::Batch; use svod_tk::kernels::gemm::{Epilogue, GemmCfg, GemmSpec, gemm}; use svod_tk::launch::graph_launch; let (m, n, k) = (1000, 512, 256); let target = Target::for_device(&default_device()).expect("a GPU target"); let device = Device { costs: svod_tk::probe::costs(&target)?.costs, target }; let cfg = GemmCfg { tile: [64, 64, 32], stages: 2, warps: [2, 2], unroll: true, core: Core::Warp, crews: 1 }; let spec = GemmSpec { m, n, k, batch: Batch::Static(1), epilogue: Epilogue::default(), cfg }; let a = Tensor::empty(&[m * k], DType::BFloat16); let b = Tensor::empty(&[n * k], DType::BFloat16); let c = Tensor::empty(&[m * n], DType::BFloat16); let c = graph_launch(gemm::<BF16>(&spec), &cfg.lowering(&device), &[&a, &b, &c])?; c.realize()?; Models do not do this themselves: ops::linear picks the config, shapes the output and falls back to the graph when the kernel does not apply.

Group Calls Declarations param, var (a launch variable bound by name), grid, warps (a count, a column of warps, or a WarpGrid the register tiles spread over), smem Scalars block(axis), warp(), row() (inside a gather map), load_scalar(param, index), Sc operators and min/max/lt/le/eq/and/or Views view, gather (a row-mapped view), periodic (columns repeating a table), at, narrow, smem_view, smem_view_as, smem_slot Tile ops fill, zeros, splat, coord, unary, binary (a row or column vector broadcasts), scale, compare (CmpOp), cast, cast_toward_zero, where_, mul_add (one rounding), reduce, reduce_f32, transpose, shift (one step along an axis, a fill first), flip (each element exchanged across a mask's bits along an axis: a sorting network's step, a rotary half's partner), mma, mma_oriented, pin Movement stage (global → shared, CopyMode::Async or Sync), load, load_as_fill, store Control loop_ (carried register tiles), pipeline, if_, select_if (branches producing tiles), where_any (a where_ whose taken side only the warps holding a set predicate element compute), each_warp (a Warps statement), barrier

Every kernel in svod_tk::kernels is a function fn k<T: Elem>(spec: &Spec) -> Program, generic over the 16-bit element type (BF16 or F16); gemm and nearest also take 8-bit integers (I8, accumulated exactly in i32: gemm stores f32, nearest scales each row's products by the rows' x_scale and c_scale). Each spec has a batch: Batch: Batch::Static(n) launches n batches, and Batch::var(name, min, max) (an ir::Var) launches the live count of a runtime variable bound by name, with buffers sized for max. Each config type has a lowering(&device) (an atoms::Device: the target and its costs). Models reach these kernels through the op layer, which picks the config. Kernel Spec → program Kernel name Op GEMM + epilogue GemmSpec → gemm::gemm gemm ops::linear Implicit-GEMM convolution ConvSpec → conv::conv (+ gemm::split_merge when split) conv, split_merge ops::conv2d Flash attention forward AttnSpec → attention::attention flash_attention ops::attention Split merge CombineSpec → attention::combine combine_splits ops::attention with splits Attention prologue HeadsSpec → heads::heads heads ops::heads LayerNorm / RMSNorm NormSpec → rows::norm layer_norm / rms_norm ops::{layer_norm, rms_norm, add_*}

c = scale·act(a·bᵀ + bias) + residual, with a [batch·m, k] and b [n, k]. Everything after the matrix product runs on the f32 accumulator, and the result is rounded once at the store. Epilogue field Effect bias [n] row added to the accumulator ([2n] when gated) act Act::None, Act::Gelu (erf approximation, error at most 1.5e-7), Act::Silu gated b is [2n, k], gate rows over up rows; output act(gate)·up (SwiGLU, GeGLU) scale Multiplies the activated value before the residual residual [batch·m, n] added last out_f32 f32 output and residual, the accumulator stored unrounded rope Rope { heads, head_dim, seq }: the first heads heads of head_dim columns rotated by [seq, head_dim/2] cos and sin tables (output row m at position m % seq), the columns after them stored as they are; with a bias alone, on a tile whose warps hold whole heads (GemmCfg::turns) GemmCfg { tile: [bm, bn, bk], stages, warps: [rows, cols], unroll, core, crews }. Rows past m and columns past n are bounded views, so m and n are free. k must be a multiple of bk. core: Core::Group issues the products on wgmma (sm_90); crews: 2 runs the two warp rows in ping-pong over one slot (CDNA). The blocks walk the output tiles in groups of 8 tile rows (gemm::GROUP_ROWS), so blocks resident together read the same B tiles. The rotation reads each element's partner half a head along through a column flip. When a warp's columns hold whole heads, a lane holds both halves, and the flip is a register renaming. The tables are read through a periodic view, so every head of a row reads the same [head_dim/2] row. The turn is not free in the ranking: its operations and the tables' reads are claimed beside the epilogue's, and a tile that holds no whole heads is refused. There is no tile table. config::Planner::gemm_ranked enumerates tiles, bk, warp grids, ring depths and unrolling, keeps what the lowering runs on the target (the atoms tile the warp grid, the fills split into whole 16-byte chunks per thread, the ring fits shared memory) and ranks the rest in nanoseconds of SM time from the device's measured Costs. Every device input to the ranking is measured; its few model constants (BAND, CACHE_SHARE, CACHE_SPILL, OVERLAP_WAVES in ops::config) are meant to hold for every device. The ranking orders, and the tuner measures the first 64 tiles that compile without spilling (Tuning).

conv::conv is an implicit GEMM over channels-last x [b, h, w, cin] and w [cout, kh, kw, cin]: A is a row-mapped view of the image (conv::im2col_view), so padding rows read zero and nothing is materialized. K = kh·kw·cin runs as one pipeline, each step inside one tap (bk divides cin). On a starved grid of a single static batch, ConvCfg::split splits K over grid z and gemm::split_merge applies the epilogue. ops::conv2d takes a 1×1 as linear and keeps groups ≠ 1, cin off 16 and cout off 8 on the graph.

o = softmax(q·kᵀ·scale + bias)·v over sequence-major q [batch, t, heads, d] and k, v [batch, tk, kv_heads, d]. Q stays in registers and K/V stream through a shared ring. The online-softmax state (m, l, o) is carried in f32 using exp2. Feature How GQA Query head h reads KV head h / (heads / kv_heads) Cross attention tk ≠ t is a property of the views Any t, tk Bounds instead of padding: the query tile and the last key block are bounded views, and keys past tk are masked Head dims Any d both products tile, whose fills split into whole chunks per thread (FaCfg::fits); the models use 48, 64 and 128 AttnMask::causal Key blocks past the diagonal are skipped through the trip count AttnMask::window (left, right) around each query; blocks outside are skipped AttnMask::chunk Block attention: a query sees its chunk, left chunks before (all, without a bound) and right after AttnMask::key_lens [batch] i32 valid key counts; blocks past the length are skipped AttnMask::key_mask [batch, tk] i32 visible keys (row stride rounded up to 8), read in every block AttnMask::seg_start [batch, t] i32 segment starts of packed rows, non-decreasing along t AttnMask::bias [batch or 1, heads, t, tk] additive bias in the stream type (row stride rounded up to 8), added to the scaled scores before the masks Only key blocks that a causal, window, chunk, length or segment edge crosses compute the predicate; blocks fully inside run unmasked. A key mask and a bias are read in every block. A query that sees no key yields zeros, as the graph writes it. Cache mode (AttnSpec::cache = Some(Cache { .. })) reads K and V from a cache [rows, tk, heads_total, d] that holds several layers' heads: Cache field Effect rows, heads_total The cache's shape row_map A [batch] i32 parameter: the cache row each batch lane reads appended Rows of [batch, appended, kv_heads, d] keys and values scored after the cached prefix (the tokens a decoder step just projected), at most a key block app_lens A [batch] i32 parameter of visible appended rows The first of this attention's heads is a [1] i32 head_start parameter, so every layer runs one program. Packed mode (AttnSpec::packed) reads q, k and v from one [batch, t, heads + 2·kv_heads, d] parameter, a fused projection, at head offsets 0, heads and heads + kv_heads, without a cache. The kernel is flash_attention_packed, tuned apart from the split one; on the same config both compute the same bits. Key splits (FaCfg::splits > 1) give a few long rows, such as a decoder step, more blocks. Each split writes f32 partials o_part, m_part and l_part, and combine merges them. Attn::splits = Some(n) fixes the count; with None, Planner::splits proposes 1, 2, the counts around two blocks per SM and one split per key block, and the tuner times each split candidate together with its merge. FaCfg { bq, bkv, stages, splits, unroll, forms, key_warps, warp_rows, core }: Field Effect warp_rows Query rows per warp: 16 (one atom row) or 32 (each K and V fragment feeds two atom rows); the 32-row form is a variant the tuner times beside its 16-row tile key_warps A one-row-warp block (bq = 16, offered for t ≤ 16) splits its key blocks over 1, 2 or 4 warps, each with its own ring slots and softmax state, merged through shared memory core Core::Group runs both products on wgmma (sm_90) forms The softmax forms below Candidates come from the same lattice and cost model as the GEMM's (Planner::attention_ranked). Where the fill goes through registers, the value tile is stored column-major so its fragments gather as 16-byte loads; on RDNA4 the fill itself is a transposing load (global_load_tr_b128). The softmax adopts a new running maximum only when it grows by more than 8 in log2 units (FlashAttention-4's lazy rescale). Five Forms are tuner knobs, all off as planned; the tuner flips each where it measures faster (a forms pass, then the tiles under those forms, then the forms again on the winner): Forms field Effect truncate_p bf16 probabilities are truncated rather than rounded, and the row sum adds what is held sum_after The row sum follows the P·V product rather than preceding the rescale skip_rescale The output's rescale is a Scale, skipped by every wave whose rows all kept their maximum raw_max The running maximum stays in the raw scores' units: a multiply per row rather than per score bias_direct Each key block's bias tile is read from global memory in the scores' layout rather than through a ring slot

heads splits a fused projection qkv [batch, t, (heads + 2·kv_heads)·d] into sequence-major q [batch, t, heads, d] and k, v [batch, t, kv_heads, d]. Optionally it RMS-normalizes q and k over the head with [d] weights, then applies rotary embedding to them. The rotation pairs the head's two halves, using (cos, sin) tables of [t, d/2], shared or per batch (Rope { per_batch }). A block handles br rows of one head slot. d must be a power of two in 16..=256, and candidates are br ∈ {4, 8, 16}.

rows::norm uses one warp per row and a fused reduce-then-map in f32: Norm Formula Layer (x − mean)·rsqrt(var + eps)·w + b Rms x·rsqrt(mean(x²) + eps)·w With residual: true it normalizes x + residual rounded to the element type and also writes that sum, which is the pre-norm residual stream of a transformer layer. d must be a multiple of 256 in 256..=2048, and candidates are br ∈ {4, 8, 16} rows per block.

lower::lower(program, &lowering, params, device) turns a tile program into a Svod program whose instruction list is already in order. A Lowering holds what the program does not say: the Device (the target and its costs) and which matrix instruction the products issue on (core): Lowering::new(&device) for the warp-level core, GemmCfg::lowering and FaCfg::lowering for their config's. The WarpGrid over the block tile (Kernel::warps) and each ring's schedule (pipeline's Ring) are the program's own; shared rows are always XOR-swizzled. lower::standalone(program, &lowering) lowers for a target with no device attached, and lower::render returns the LLVM text the backend's compiler would be handed. Step Module Effect 1. Operand materialization lower A shared or global mma operand gets an explicit load into a fresh register tile; on the warpgroup core shared operands stay in place 2. Barriers lower::sync Shared-memory effects are fenced: barriers, and a commit and wait before an async copy's tile is used. A Pipeline is still one statement whose template fences its own ring, so the pass fences only where the ring meets the code around it 3. Schedule expansion schedule::expand Every Pipeline becomes loops, branches and explicit Sync statements 4. Layout inference layouts::infer Every register tile gets a layout; conflicts get a Relayout 5. Shared orientation lower A shared allocation filled through registers is stored along the axis its readers' fragments run along, so a gather is 16-byte loads; cp.async tiles stay row-major 6. Emission lower/emit/ Statements are emitted in program order into UOp::linear_program lower fails with Error::Grid when the program's warps are not the warp grid's, or a multiple of it with a Warps statement in the body, and with Error::DivergentBarrier when a block barrier sits under a branch on the warp, which some warps would skip.

A layout::Layout is a linear map over GF(2) from the bits of input dimensions to the bits of output dimensions (the "Linear Layouts" formulation of Triton). The dimensions are Dim::{Reg, Lane, Warp, Block, Row, Col}. The map stores one basis vector per input bit. Every vendor fragment, every XOR swizzle and every ldmatrix plan is such a map. This is the PTX mma.m16n8k16 accumulator, from layout/atoms.rs: /// PTX `mma.m16n8k16` C/D fragment (16×8, M×N): `row = g + 8·(c/2), col = 2t + c%2`. pub fn mma_sync_c() -> Layout { Layout::from_bases( [(Row, 16), (Col, 8)], &[(Reg, &[[0, 1], [8, 0]]), (Lane, &[[0, 2], [0, 4], [1, 0], [2, 0], [4, 0]])], ) } The algebra has identity, zeros, from_bases, transpose, product (tile one layout over another), sublayout and apply. The tests check every atom against the lane formulas of the vendor ISA documents (test/unit/atoms.rs) and against tk1's closed forms (test/unit/layout.rs). A register tile's layout is a layouts::TileLayout { frag, reps, warps }. It holds a fragment over (Reg, Lane), repeated reps times inside each warp's sub-tile, with the warps' sub-tile coordinates.

An atoms::MmaAtom is one matrix-core instruction with the layouts of its a, b and c operands. Target::mma(dtype_in, dtype_out) finds it. A kernel never names one: the inference reads the operand layouts from the atom that consumes the values. Target Atom (bf16/f16 → f32) Fragment layouts CUDA mma.sync m16n8k16 mma_sync_a, mma_sync_b, mma_sync_c CUDA sm_90 wgmma m64nNk16, four warps at once wgmma_a, wgmma_c; B through a descriptor, never held AMD CDNA MFMA 16×16×16 mfma_16x16x16 AMD RDNA3 / RDNA4 WMMA 16×16×16 wmma_gfx11_input, wmma_gfx11_acc / wmma_gfx12 Apple simdgroup 8×8×8 (atom only; no kernels) simdgroup_8x8 Each target with kernels also has an 8-bit integer atom into i32 (Target::geometry_of(Int8)): mma.sync m16n8k32 s8 and CDNA's MFMA 16×16×32 i8 hold the 16-bit fragments' bytes, twice as deep (mma_sync_a8, mma_sync_b8, mfma_16x16x32_i8); RDNA's iu8 WMMA keeps the 16-bit layouts at depth 16. Its m and n are the 16-bit atom's. The planner prices the 16-bit geometry (Target::geometry) except for a problem over 8-bit rows. An atoms::GroupMmaAtom is a warpgroup instruction: four consecutive warps issue a 64 × n product together over operands read from shared memory through descriptors (B always, A unless it is a register tile), the accumulator spread over the group with each warp holding 16 rows in the mma.sync C layout. A config whose core is Core::Group lowers its products on it: the grid's rows are warpgroups, shared operands stay in place instead of being loaded, and the emitter writes each product as one wgmma chain over the ring's swizzled rows (the descriptor's swizzle mode is the lowering's own XOR, layouts::Swizzle). The GEMM and attention configs both offer this core on sm_90.

Atoms seed. An mma gives its operands and result the atom's layouts tiled over the WarpGrid (MmaAtom::issue), issued whichever way round (ir::Orient) leaves the program the least relayout cost under the lowering's Costs: Cᵀ = Bᵀ·Aᵀ is the same instruction with its slots exchanged, so on a square atom an accumulator can be held as the next product's operand at no cost. A product whose result is dealt (TileOp::Deal, a list's lane queues) is issued the way round that spreads a row over the fewest lanes (MmaAtom::narrow), where a deal renames registers, as the op layer prices it. An author may pin the orientation (Kernel::mma_oriented). Elementwise ops unify. Operands and the result of binary, cast, where_, mul_add and the carried values of a loop share one layout. Unconstrained tiles take a natural layout. At a fixed point, a tile nothing constrains gets layouts::natural: each lane holds a short row vector of up to 8 elements, lanes walk the columns then the rows, and warps split the rows. Vectors follow their tile. A [rows, 1] or [1, cols] vector, such as the output of a reduce or a bias row, is demanded in the row or column layout its tile implies. Conflicts become relayouts. A value two consumers want differently gets a TileOp::Relayout. TileLayout::relayout classifies it as Identity, RegPermute (within each lane, free), Exchange (each register taken by lane-xor moves from fixed partners) or ViaSmem. An Exchange is kept only while its work costs less than a round trip through shared memory (Relayout::work × Costs::lane_move < Costs::smem_trip). The emitter lowers an Exchange with the target's atoms::LaneMove (shfl.sync on CUDA, DPP and permlanex16 on RDNA, ds_bpermute on CDNA). A flip moves by the same classes: in each lane where it holds both exchanged elements (a register renaming), else by the lane moves of TileLayout::flip; partners another warp holds are unsupported, and a turning GEMM's ranking admits only tiles whose warps hold whole heads.

schedule::expand runs each Pipeline by its Ring { stages, unroll, crews } and the target's Fill. One crew: every warp loads and computes. Two crews: the block's warps as two crews a cluster apart over one register-staged slot (CDNA GEMM, GemmCfg::crews == 2). Fill Expansion of pipeline(extent, ring, …) Fill::CpAsync, stages ≥ 2 One loop of extent + stages − 1 iterations. Each iteration waits until at most stages − 2 copy groups are pending, then barriers and consumes step i − (stages − 1). It then issues step i's cp.async copies into the slot freed one iteration earlier and commits them as one group (an empty group past the end keeps the count uniform). Fill::CpAsync, stages ≥ 3, warpgroup core, a consume whose products only feed products The same, with the consume's wgmma chains left in flight over the next fill: the slot consumed two trips ago is refilled, and after each consume every thread waits for all but its youngest chain (Sync::WaitProducts). Fill::CpAsync, stages = 1 Copy, wait, consume, and a barrier before the slot is refilled. Fill::Staged, 2 stages Three loops over one induction variable: the first trip loads step 0 into registers and stores it to its slot; a steady trip loads step i into registers, fences, consumes step i − 1, fences, and stores the registers to step i's slot, with no branch in its body (the fences keep the loads ahead of the products and the commit behind them on RDNA); the last trip only consumes. Fill::Staged, 1 stage The same three loops over one slot: the store waits behind a barrier for every warp to finish the slot, then barriers again, so a tile twice as deep fits the same shared memory. two crews A trip is cut at its products into load clusters and product clusters, a block barrier after each, so one crew's products run from registers at raised issue priority while the other crew loads. unroll copies the loop body once per ring slot so slot arithmetic folds to constants; the tuner measures both. Async and staged copies belong to the template, which fences them. The lower::sync pass covers the rest: a shared tile written by a synchronous copy is fenced before another thread reads it, and a tile read since the last fence is fenced before it is overwritten.

The emitter lists every statement's instructions in program order inside a pre-linearized program, so Svod's linearizer toposort never runs on a tk kernel. Global accesses past a view's bounds are gated: loads read zero and stores are dropped. Shared rows are XOR-swizzled in 16-byte chunks where the row's chunk count is a power of two (layouts::Swizzle). Shared to register loads of 16-bit tiles use ldmatrix.x4 where the layout allows, and of 8-bit ones its untransposed form over 16×32 bytes; on RDNA4 global to register loads use global_load_tr_b128 where the layout is what it leaves. A Warps statement runs its body on each warp alone, with its own copies and barriers. On AMD an f32 exp2 is the hardware v_exp_f32, which flushes results below 2⁻¹²⁶ to zero. Shared memory above 48 KB is one dynamic array on CUDA; candidates are filtered against Target::smem_bytes. Invariants kept by the emitter, not the author Pure values are listed at the loop level their inputs require. Register accesses are scalar. Shared and global accesses are SHRINK vector accesses. Gated stores sit inside an If. Carried values move into their phi at the end of the block that defines them. A loop whose extent may fall below zero runs no trip (the range's end is floored). TK_DUMP_LIST=1 prints the emitted list (see Testing and Debugging).

svod_tk::ops is what models call. Every op returns a lazy Tensor. When the device, dtypes and shapes fit a kernel, a tk kernel computes it. Otherwise the op builds the equivalent graph itself. A model never checks whether a kernel applies and never pads to a tile. pub fn linear(x: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, opts: Linear) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn conv2d(x: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, opts: Conv) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn attention(q: &Tensor, k: &Tensor, v: &Tensor, opts: Attn) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn attention_packed(qkv: &Tensor, heads: usize, kv_heads: usize, opts: Attn) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn heads(qkv: &Tensor, opts: Qkv) -> Result<(Tensor, Tensor, Tensor)>; pub fn layer_norm(x: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, b: Option<&Tensor>, eps: f64) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn add_layer_norm(x: &Tensor, residual: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, b: Option<&Tensor>, eps: f64) -> Result<(Tensor, Tensor)>; pub fn rms_norm(x: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, eps: f64) -> Result<Tensor>; pub fn add_rms_norm(x: &Tensor, residual: &Tensor, w: &Tensor, eps: f64) -> Result<(Tensor, Tensor)>; pub fn supported(device: &DeviceSpec) -> bool; Op Shapes Options attention q [B, T, H, D], k/v [B, Tk, H_kv, D] → [B, T, H, D] Attn { causal, keys, window, chunk, seg_start, cache, splits, scale, bias } attention_packed qkv [B, T, (H + 2·H_kv)·D] → [B, T, H, D] Attn without a cache; heads, kv_heads linear x [lead..., K], w [N, K] → [lead..., N] Linear { bias, act, gated, residual, scale, rope }; gated w is [2N, K] conv2d x [B, H, W, Cin], w [Cout, kh, kw, Cin / groups] → [B, Ho, Wo, Cout] Conv { stride, pad, dilation, groups, bias, act, residual, scale, out_dtype }; a 1×1 is linear heads qkv [B, T, (H + 2·H_kv)·D] → q, k, v Qkv { heads, kv_heads, head_dim, q_norm, k_norm, eps, rope } layer_norm, rms_norm x [..., D], w/b [D] add_* take residual like x and return (x + residual, norm) Linear::scale multiplies the activated value before the residual add: scale·act(x·wᵀ + bias) + residual, so a Conformer half-step x + 0.5·ffn(x) is one GEMM. Linear::rope is Rotary { cos, sin, heads, head_dim }: the output's first heads heads of head_dim columns are rotated after the bias by (cos, sin) tables of [1, T, 1, head_dim/2], the head's two halves paired as apply_rotary_emb pairs them, for x [B, T, K]. Beside an activation, a residual or a scale the whole linear runs on the graph. Otherwise the GEMM rotates them in its store when the tables share x's dtype and a tile holds whole heads per warp, and if not, a plain GEMM runs and the graph rotates its output. attention_packed then reads such a projection's queries, keys and values in place, where heads would copy them out. Attn::keys is KeyMask::None, KeyMask::Lens(&lens) ([B] valid key counts) or KeyMask::Bool(&mask) ([B, Tk], true where attended). Attn::cache takes Cache { head_start, kv_heads, row_map, appended, app_lens }, and appended requires KeyMask::Lens. Attn::chunk is block attention (Chunk { size, left, right }). Attn::scale defaults to 1/√D. Attn::bias ([B, H, T, Tk] or [1, H, T, Tk], the stream dtype) is added to the scaled scores before the masks, as in WavLM's relative position bias. Qkv::rope is (cos, sin) of [1, T, 1, D/2] (by position) or [B, T, 1, D/2] (by token). The masks are described with the attention kernel.

The decision is a pure function in ops::shape, fn(planner, dtypes, extents, …) -> Plan<Cfg>, so it is tested on the host without a GPU (test/unit/ops_plan.rs). Plan::Kernel(configs) holds the ranked configs; the tuner measures the first that compile without spilling (or, when every one spills, the first that compile: spills never send an op to the graph). Plan::Graph(Fallback) says why the graph runs, and the planner log names it (RUST_LOG=svod_tk::plan=debug). Fallback When Target The tensor is not on the default device, the device has no tk kernels (config::has_kernels: CUDA below sm_80, Metal, the CPU), or its target reports no SM count Dtype Any operand is f32, or the operands do not all share one 16-bit type with a matrix core (nearest and k_nearest also take i8 rows, each scaled by 1). conv2d: an output type other than the input's or f32, or a residual not in it Symbolic A dim other than a bound leading one is symbolic (for linear, also a symbolic N) Shape linear: N not a multiple of 8 or no rows. conv2d: groups > 1, Cin not a multiple of 16, Cout not a multiple of 8, or an empty output. attention: no config fits D (on sm_86, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256 plan and 40 does not) or an empty dim. heads: D not a power of two in 16..=256. Norms: D not a multiple of 256 in 256..=2048 Config No tile config fits. For linear, K is not a multiple of 16 attention also takes the graph when appended rows are wider than every config's key block. ops::chosen() returns what the last op this thread ran chose, as a value beside the tensors it returned: Chosen::Kernel { op, family, cfg } — the kernel's name (family) and its pick's Debug text (cfg), which names a nearest pick's path (score matrix, queue, splits) — or Chosen::Graph { op, why }. k_nearest_reranked's record is its search's: the winning rows' dtype beside its config. Why f32 keeps the graph The kernels take 16-bit operands (and, for the nearest-neighbour search, 8-bit integers). Casting an f32 model down would trade about three decimal digits of precision for speed, so the op layer leaves that choice to the model's dtype. k_nearest_reranked is the exception that keeps f32 numbers: it searches the rows in 8 bits or f16 (Quantized with its QuantScheme::Row scale, Rerank), keeps each row's k + margin least (16 by default), and scores those again in f32 from the rows as given. Rerank::search names the rows (Search::Int8, Search::Half(f16), or Search::Auto, the faster of the two — which one won is the op's chosen() record). A neighbour the search ranks past k + margin is missed.

Dim 0 of an operand may be symbolic when it is bound to a runtime variable. That variable is either the JIT's batch_var or a DefineVar/bounded Param with min and max. The kernel then launches over the live count in grid z, and its buffers hold the maximum. Outputs are allocated at capacity with the symbolic dim kept in their shape (Tensor::empty_dynamic_spec). The next kernel therefore binds the realized buffer itself, and no copy is made to shrink it. Any other symbolic dim is Fallback::Symbolic.

Err is reserved for what the graph op would also reject, plus a failed kernel build: ops::Error Meaning Shape { op, operand, got, expected } An operand's shape does not fit the op Dtype { op, operand, got, want } w (or k, v, norm weights, rope tables) differs from the input's dtype Heads { op, heads, kv_heads } heads is not a multiple of kv_heads Graph { op, source } Building the graph fallback failed Launch { op, source } Lowering or binding the kernel failed

Nemotron-3-Diarization's self-attention, from model/src/nemotron_diar/model.rs: one stacked QKV projection, the fused prologue with RoPE, attention under key lengths, and the output projection with the residual in its epilogue. fn forward(&self, x: &Tensor, rope: &(Tensor, Tensor), key_lens: &Tensor, residual: &Tensor) -> Result<Tensor> { let (b, s, d) = (x.dim(0)?, x.dim(1)?, x.dim_const(2)?); let qkv = ops::linear(x, &self.qkv_weight, ops::Linear::default())?; let (cos, sin) = rope; let split = Qkv { heads: self.num_heads, kv_heads: self.num_heads, head_dim: d / self.num_heads, q_norm: None, k_norm: None, eps: 0.0, rope: Some((cos, sin)), }; let (q, k, v) = ops::heads(&qkv, split)?; let opts = Attn { keys: KeyMask::Lens(key_lens), ..Attn::default() }; let out = ops::attention(&q, &k, &v, opts)?; project(&self.o_proj, &out.try_reshape([b, s, SInt::Const(d)])?, Act::None, Some(residual)) } project is ops::linear with the layer's bias, an activation and an optional residual. The same file runs its LayerNorms through ops::layer_norm.

Svod's optimizer finds fast schedules for most of a model by searching over loop transformations. Some kernels cannot be found that way. Flash attention is a recurrence: every key block updates a running maximum and sum and rescales the accumulator, so there is no single reduction to tile. A fast GEMM on a tensor-core GPU depends on a multi-stage cp.async ring, ldmatrix fragment loads and a swizzled shared layout, which are not steps of a loop search. Kernels like these are written by hand, and svod-tk ("tk") is the crate for writing them. svod-tk implements the third version of the tile language ("tk3") and is the only tile-kernel crate. It replaced tk1, the earlier crate of the same name, which was removed together with its k-means, kNN and Apple kernels; none of them was ported. Eight models run on the op layer: Nemotron-3-Diarization, Whisper (the encoder, and the decoder step's attention in cache mode), ModernBERT, BGE-M3/XLM-RoBERTa, Qwen3-Embedding, GigaAM, WavLM and YOLO26 (channels-last, its 3×3 convolutions on ops::conv2d).

atoms::Target holds what a GPU can do: its matrix-core atoms, how global memory reaches a shared ring (Fill::CpAsync or Fill::Staged), ldmatrix and transposing loads, lane moves, which syncs are instructions (SyncCaps), occupancy, shared memory and SM count; see its rustdoc. Target::for_device(&spec) resolves a target from a live device, Target::for_arch from an architecture alone (what host tests use), and Target::offline(arch, sms, xcds) or Target::card(name) describes a card this machine has no device for. A target declares what the chip can do, never what it costs. What its primitives cost (atoms::Costs) is measured on the device at first use (probe::costs) and kept in the tune store; host tests declare it (Tuning). There are no per-family cost tables. The costs reach the lowering as Lowering::device (orientation, exchange or round trip) and the op layer as the Planner's device (the candidate rankings). The measured targets and their numbers are in the Overview. ops::supported(device) is true when device is the default device, its target has tk kernels (config::has_kernels) and reports an SM count; the cost probes run on the first ask. On any other device each op builds its graph fallback (Fallback::Target). Host tests check every atom's operand layouts against the lane formulas of the vendor ISA documents, and for each target with kernels they lower every kernel family, interpret it before and after lowering, and compile it with ptxas or clang when those are installed. "Compiled" is not "correct on the device": a target is measured only once targets::families_match_the_interpreter_on_the_device passes on its hardware. Without cp.async (AMD has no asynchronous global → LDS copy) a pipeline loads each step into registers, computes the previous step, then writes the registers to shared memory, over one or two slots. The same path runs on CUDA in a device test (register_staged_families_match_on_cuda).

The decided approach is one shared tile program per op. A kernel such as kernels/gemm.rs is written once against tile values and never branches on the vendor. What varies per target is data the lowering and the op layer choose: Per target Where Matrix-core atoms and their layouts atoms, layout/atoms.rs Copy mechanisms (cp.async, ldmatrix, register staging, transposing loads) Target fields, the emitter Schedule templates schedule::Schedule Config candidate rankings ops::config, from the measured Costs A forked kernel program for one vendor is allowed only as a bounded exception.

Each tk kernel is checked at two levels. On the host, its tile program runs in the interpreter against a direct reference, and the lowered program renders and, where the toolchain is installed, compiles for every target. On a GPU with tk kernels (CUDA or AMD), the lowered kernel runs against the interpreter or against the op's own graph fallback. Tests compare values within tolerances, not hashes of the IR.

interp::run(&program, params, vars) executes a tile program on the host. It takes one Vec<f64> per parameter and returns every parameter after the run. Each block runs its statements in order, and a pipeline runs as its serial interleaving. Every value is rounded to its element type (interp::round_to), so the result is what a correct lowering must reproduce up to accumulation order. Scalar division truncates toward zero, as the emitted code does. Runtime variables are bound by name: let out = run(&prog, vec![a.clone(), b.clone(), vec![0.0; m * n]], &[("b", 1)]).unwrap(); It returns interp::Error::{UnboundVar, ParamSize, Division, OutOfBounds}: an access past a buffer's capacity is an error, not a silent read. It does not model threads or barriers, so ordering bugs show up only on the device.

SVOD_DEVICE selects the device. Device tests skip with a skipped: … line only where there is nothing to run on: SVOD_DEVICE=CPU, a GPU tk has no kernels for, or no SVOD_DEVICE and no supported GPU attached. With a supported GPU attached and SVOD_DEVICE unset, they fail and name the value to set, since a suite whose device tests all skip passes and proves nothing. # Host only, no GPU: SVOD_DEVICE=CPU cargo test -p svod-tk --release --lib # On the GPU; on a fresh tune store run the cost probes alone first, since the parallel # suite inflates what they measure and the store keeps the first measurement: SVOD_DEVICE=CUDA cargo test -p svod-tk --release --lib device_costs_are_physical SVOD_DEVICE=CUDA cargo test -p svod-tk --release --lib SVOD_DEVICE=AMD (or AMD:N, in KFD node order) selects an AMD GPU. A target counts as measured only once families_match_the_interpreter_on_the_device passes on it: every family's first candidate on the device against the interpreter. register_staged_families_match_on_cuda runs the AMD data path (register-staged fills, no ldmatrix) on a CUDA GPU.

Point the tune store at a directory to keep: SVOD_TK_TUNE_DIR=$PWD/tk_tune_$(hostname). On a machine with several AMD nodes, check that the node SVOD_DEVICE=AMD:N names is the GPU (/sys/class/kfd/kfd/topology/nodes/*/properties, gfx_target_version). Run device_costs_are_physical alone, then families_match_the_interpreter_on_the_device, then the suite. Do not report numbers for a device whose gate fails. The model-level gate for Nemotron (real weights, generated goldens): SVOD_DEVICE=CUDA cargo test -p svod-model --release --lib nemotron_diar::parity::half_precision -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1

An op that falls back builds graph ops instead of a CALL; the ops.rs tests look for the kernel's name among the calls of the result's graph. To predict the path without a device, call the ops::shape planner (see Op Layer); on a device, the planner log says why an op took the graph (Tuning).

The tk_dump example shows what tk would run on a card this machine has no device for: the planner's ranking with predicted ns and why each config of the lattice was left out (plan.txt), the chosen config's LLVM text and, where the tools are installed, its PTX, ptxas -v resources and SASS (CUDA) or AMDGCN assembly with its resource comments (AMD), and an opcode histogram of the main loop. cargo run -p svod-tk --release --example tk_dump -- --card h100-pcie --op gemm --shape 4096x4096x4096 cargo run -p svod-tk --release --example tk_dump -- --arch gfx942 --op attention --shape 8x16x1024x128 --causal --store DIR --card takes a name of atoms::CARDS (rtx3060, h100-pcie, h100-sxm, rtx5070, rtx5090, mi300x, mi355x, rx9070xt, strix-halo); --arch takes an architecture with --sms/--xcds or the first listed card's. --store is a tune store directory copied from the card, whose probe lines price the ranking; without it the guessed costs do. --cfg N emits the N-th ranked config, --out DIR names the output directory (tk_dump). --op takes gemm (--shape MxNxK), attention (BxHxTxD), norm (RxD), conv (BxHxWxCINxCOUT) or heads (BxTxHxKVxD), each through the op layer's own shape gate and tuning. --cfg tuned emits the config the tuner chose on the card, read from the --store copy without writing to it: a stored line matches by op, device, dtype, shape and the config list the op layer keys it by, whatever compiler or kernel build wrote it, and the dump prints each key it read or says which line is missing. --compare FILE [--fun NAME] prints the main loop of a reference kernel (a .cubin, an AMD code object, or SASS, PTX or AMDGCN text) beside tk's, counted the same way. cargo run -p svod-tk --release --example tk_dump -- --card rtx3060 --op gemm --shape 4096x4096x4096 --cfg tuned --store ~/.cache/svod/tk_tune cargo run -p svod-tk --release --example tk_dump -- --card mi300x --op gemm --shape 4096x4096x4096 --compare hk.co --fun NAME
